messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was a 33-year-old African American man who worked as a tailor in a small shop near a busy transit corridor, where the steady hum of traffic outside and the constant coming and going of customers had once felt ordinary. That changed after the bombing at the market two years earlier, when he had gone to buy fabric and heard the blast tear through the crowd several stalls away. He remembered the bright flash, the choking dust, people shouting, and the terrible confusion of not knowing where the danger was coming from. Since then, the memory of that day had not stayed in one piece. At times he could picture fragments with almost film-like clarity, as if the scene kept replaying without his permission; at other moments he reached for details and found blank spaces he could not fill, and sometimes he could recall it only with a strange numbness, as though it had happened to somebody else entirely. The gaps and the replay both fed his conviction that something essential in him had broken. The more he sat with that conviction, the more the memory seemed to catch and return on its own, as if his mind kept dragging him back to the worst minutes at the market to prove how damaged he felt. Telling himself he had failed to protect himself made the fragments sharper and easier to find, and the replay became another way of confirming that he could not trust his own strength. He came to believe he could not trust himself to do the right thing if something happened again, and that belief hardened into the sense that he was weak and did not really belong anywhere anymore.

In the months after the bombing, Kwame began organizing his days around the feeling that he was not safe in the world. That constant sense of danger gradually hardened into the beliefs that he was weak, broken, and no longer really belonged anywhere secure, because feeling afraid all the time seemed to him like proof that something in him had changed for good. Whenever he entered the tailoring shop, a bus, a church hall, or even a client’s house, he scanned for exits first and made sure he could sit with his back against a wall where he could see the whole room. He was constantly on guard, watching faces, hands, doors, and windows, as if danger might arrive without warning. The memory of the market attack made those habits feel necessary rather than excessive: if he had missed the threat once, he told himself, he might miss it again. That same terror also made him feel small and unreliable, as though a strong person would have protected himself or others better. In that state, he withdrew from the future almost entirely. He stopped making plans beyond the next day and avoided speaking about work projects, travel, or saving money, because imagining a future felt like tempting fate. When the unease became unbearable, he escaped into long stretches on his phone, games, and internet videos, letting hours disappear so he would not have to think. At other times he picked arguments with his sister, a cousin, or even customers, creating drama that gave his mind something immediate to focus on instead of the terror underneath.

Over time, the ways he tried to outrun the memory began to pull him further into it. A loud bang from a dropped spool of thread, the smell of dust from fabric bolts, or the crowded doorway of the shop could bring back pieces of the bombing with startling force, and once those fragments surfaced he became even more watchful and more convinced that he was failing at being a man who could protect himself. He would replay the event mentally while staring at his phone late into the night, only to feel numb and ashamed afterward, which made him sink deeper into the same pattern of escape. The more he noticed himself avoiding the future, the more he took it as proof that he was weak and did not belong anywhere stable or secure. That belief also shaped how he spoke to others: if he felt judged, he became defensive, picking fights so people would look at his anger rather than at his fear. His shop began to suffer. He missed opportunities for larger tailoring orders because he would not commit to deadlines weeks ahead, and he started keeping conversations with regular clients brief, edgy, and transactional. The practical consequences deepened his isolation, and the isolation made the room-scanning, wall-seeking, and conflict-seeking feel even more necessary.

By the time he came for help, Kwame was exhausted by living as if every room might become the market again. He was sleeping poorly, spending much of his free time online, and noticing that his temper was straining the few relationships he still maintained. What brought him in was a recent afternoon at the shop when a sudden shout from the street made him freeze, scan the doorway, and feel the whole scene from the bombing rush back at once. He left work early and sat in his apartment with his back against the wall, staring at his phone and realizing he could not keep going like this. He said he was most afraid that he would always be trapped in that day, unable to trust himself, unable to feel he belonged anywhere, and he was most hoping that treatment might help him stop living in constant readiness for the next explosion.
